title: RBA hikes interest rates to 2008 levels, sharply raises inflation forecasts
full_text:
Investing.com-- The Reserve Bank of Australia raised interest rates to a 18-year high on Tuesday and sharply hiked its inflation expectations for the year, warning of more rate increases.
The RBA hiked its cash rate target by 25 basis points to 4.85%, in line with market expectations. The decision was not unanimous, with three of the RBA’s nine-member rate-setting board voting in favor of a hold.
The cash rate is now at its highest level since late-2008, where the RBA had aggressively hiked rates in the wake of the global financial crisis.
Tuesday’s hike is the RBA’s fifth such move this year, and comes as the central bank struggles to quash sticky Australian inflation. A mix of higher energy prices– due to the Middle East conflict– plus strong domestic demand and artificial intelligence investment drove Australian consumer price index inflation to near three-year highs this year.
Core inflation, as measured by trimmed mean CPI, also sat well above the RBA’s 2% to 3% target range.
The RBA hiked its end-2026 CPI forecast to 4.7% from a prior forecast of 3.6%. Trimmed mean CPI is expected at 3.6%, up from prior forecasts of 3.3%.
“Given the revised inflation outlook and the continuing upside risks, the Board judged that a further tightening in financial conditions is warranted to support the return of inflation to target,” the RBA said in a statement.
“Monetary policy is well placed to respond to developments, and the Board is focused on its mandate to deliver price stability and full employment.”
The central bank flagged increasing risks that higher inflation expectations will become embedded– a scenario the RBA has constantly warned against.
Still, the RBA hiked its gross domestic product forecast for 2026, to 1.6% from 1.4%.
The RBA raised its unemployment forecast to 4.7% from 4.5% by end-2026, flagging some cooling in the economy due to high rates.
The Australian dollar weakened slightly after the RBA’s hike, with the AUD/USD pair falling 0.2%.
Capital Economics analysts said Tuesday’s move showed the RBA as more confident that monetary policy was sufficiently tight, and that the central bank’s next move would be a cut.

title: China hikes forex deposit reserve ratio to 6%
full_text:
Investing.com-- The People’s Bank of China said on Tuesday it will raise the foreign exchange deposit reserve ratio for local institutions to 6% from 4%, starting November 15.
The hike is aimed at strengthening foreign exchange liquidity management by local institutions, the PBOC said in a statement.
The FX deposit reserve ratio determines the amount of dollar reserves local financial institutions are mandated to keep with the PBOC. An increase in the ratio will require local institutions to lock up an additional 2% of their dollar reserves with the central bank-- tightening domestic dollar supplies and increasing yuan liquidity.
Such a move is negative for the Chinese currency.

title: Reddit blasts Australia’s ’inept’ social media ban as court challenge begins
full_text:
By Peter Hobson
CANBERRA, Nov 3 (Reuters) - Australia’s world-first teen social media ban was "ill thought out" and amounted to a "profound restriction on political debate", a lawyer for messaging platform Reddit told the country’s top court in the first legal challenge to the law.
Reddit and a libertarian advocacy group have taken to the High Court to contest the Australian law, which bans large social media platforms from letting under-16s have an account and took effect in late 2025 amid support from parents and opposition from the tech firms.
A successful challenge could usher in more opposition from affected companies and slow a global uptake of similar policies as lawmakers from Britain to Malaysia roll out the measures in an effort to protect youth mental and physical health.
The Australian government and its communications minister, a named defendant, have said they will defend the law.
Addressing the court, Perry Herzfeld, for Reddit, said barring under-16s from holding social media accounts stopped them from creating or responding to content on what he called the most important means of communication in the modern world.
"That is a very profound restriction on political debate in Australia," Herzfeld said.
"There is a very substantial restriction on what young people can now do."
Reddit agreed with the Australians’ harm-minimisation aim but the law failed to do so, Herzfeld said, terming the legislation "ill thought out" and "inept" since it did not call for any specific measure to keep out minors and failed to restrict other online services where cyberbullying took place, such as gaming websites.
While social media content could typically only be created or commented on by logged-in account-holders, vast amounts of material were visible to people with no account, he said.
"If the Commonwealth is worried about particular features (of social media), it should regulate the features, which it has not done," he said.
Since the ban went live, multiple studies, including by Australian regulator the eSafety Commissioner, have found that most of the country’s teenagers under the cutoff age continue to use social media.
The government has since doubled the maximum fine for non-compliance to A$99 million ($69.5 million), given the eSafety Commissioner greater discovery powers, and said it is preparing an enforcement lawsuit against some of the biggest platforms.

title: European shares slide as Apple margin warning trigger global tech rout
full_text:
Investing.com - European shares dropped on Tuesday, succumbing to a worldwide sell-off across technology bourses after Apple warned of margin compression from rising chip costs, while a $20 billion capital raise by Oracle reignited investor anxiety over artificial intelligence funding and cash burn.
The pan-European STOXX 600 index fell 0.7%, while Germany’s DAX fell nearly 1%. France’s CAC 40 fell 0.5% while London’s FTSE 100 fell 0.4%. Italy’s FTSE MIB and Spain’s IBEX 35 dropped over 1% each.
The drawdown was led by the technology sector after Apple warned that persistent inflation in memory chip prices would squeeze gross margins through the crucial holiday shopping quarter.
The continent’s semiconductor ecosystem - including lithography giant ASML, assembly equipment makers ASM International and BE SemiconductoR all fell between 2% and 4% and chip suppliers STMicroelectronics and Infineon - trades as a direct proxy for global consumer electronics hardware and datacenter supply chains - fell over 3% each.
With the world’s most valuable tech platform signaling that higher component bills are eroding profitability, European semiconductor suppliers came under sharp selling pressure amid fears that hardware makers will either absorb margin compression or face demand destruction if input expenses are passed on to consumers
The hardware chill was compounded by news that enterprise software giant Oracle plans to raise $20 billion through a combination of bond and share sales to fund its aggressive cloud infrastructure and datacenter expansion.
This week, about 20% of the STOXX 600 companies are expected to report their quarterly results, marking one of the busiest stretches of the European third-quarter earnings season.
German airline group Lufthansa saw its shares gain 1.6%. The management narrowed its full-year 2026 operating profit forecast due to soaring jet fuel costs tied to Middle Eastern supply tensions.
Conversely, Dutch medical technology heavyweight Koninklijke Philips advanced 6.4% after posting higher quarterly profit.
U.S. midterms test Trump’s second-term agenda
Cross-asset flows were further restrained by caution ahead of Tuesday’s U.S. midterm elections, with American voters heading to the polls to deliver a referendum on the first two years of President Donald Trump’s second term.
A Democratic-controlled or divided Congress would introduce legislative gridlock, slowing domestic deregulatory momentum and raising the stakes for upcoming federal debt ceiling negotiations, while potentially curbing federal spending initiatives.
With investors also awaiting Friday’s October U.S. nonfarm payrolls report to gauge the Federal Reserve’s December interest-rate trajectory, dealing desks maintained low risk profiles across European bourses.

The nine-month U.S.-Iran conflict has driven energy prices higher and fuelled inflation, increasing pressure on central banks to raise interest rates.
Higher borrowing costs typically weigh on gold because it does not generate interest income. However, easing oil prices have temporarily reduced concerns about further monetary tightening.

Nov 3 (Reuters) - A fresh bout of AI anxiety pressured global stocks on Tuesday, while investors were on tenterhooks as voting began in crucial US midterm elections.
Traders on Polymarket see about a 77% chance of Democrats winning both chambers of the US Congress, an outcome that could lead to tougher oversight of AI and more corporate regulation.

Futures tracking the tech-heavy Nasdaq-100 index were broadly flat while S&P 500 contracts dropped 0.14%. The indexes fell for a third straight session on Monday.
The pan-European STOXX 600 index was down 0.6% to 645.36 points. South Korea’s KOSPI benchmark fell 3.6%, while Taiwan’s index dropped 3.6% for its steepest one-day decline since late July.
MSCI’s gauge of stocks across the globe slipped 0.26%.
The dollar index, which measures the currency against a basket of peers, dipped to 101.69. It hit a one-month low on Monday.
The yield on the US 10-year Treasury note rose 1.2 basis points to 4.9064%.

The offshore yuan weakened 0.37% to 6.6710 per dollar and its onshore counterpart fell 0.38% to 6.6731. The Taiwan dollar was among the weaker regional currencies, falling 0.6% against the greenback, while the Philippine peso and Indonesian rupiah lost 0.34% and 0.4%, respectively.
The Singapore dollar and Malaysian ringgit also weakened, while the Indian rupee was little changed at 94.918 per dollar. The yen edged higher to 157.80 per dollar in holiday-thinned Japanese trading. The New Zealand dollar gained 0.1% to $0.5629, while the euro and sterling rose 0.13% and 0.1%, respectively.
Australian dollar slips as split RBA decision points to a policy pause
The RBA raised its cash rate by 25 basis points to 4.85%, its highest level in 18 years and its fifth increase this year. However, the 6-3 vote was less unanimous than markets had anticipated, with three of the nine board members favouring an unchanged rate.
The Australian dollar fell as much as 0.4% after the decision. Capital Economics economist Marcel Thieliant said the RBA appeared more confident that policy was sufficiently tight, noting that it now described financial conditions as “restrictive” rather than “somewhat restrictive.”
The firm expects the bank to have finished raising rates, with its next move likely to be a cut, although not until late 2027.
The RBA nevertheless raised its inflation outlook, projecting trimmed mean inflation at 3.5% by mid-2027, up from its previous forecast of 3.0%. It cited higher fuel and commodity costs linked to the Middle East conflict, as well as tighter domestic capacity pressures.
The dollar also struggled to benefit from broader risk aversion. Investors are weighing Tuesday’s U.S. midterm elections and Friday’s employment report.
DBS expects October nonfarm payrolls to increase by 100,000, compared with 29,000 previously, with the data potentially influencing whether the Fed reconsiders its tightening bias.
Yuan retreats after PBOC move as won draws support from exports
The offshore yuan weakened after the People’s Bank of China announced it would raise the foreign-exchange reserve requirement ratio by two percentage points to 6% from 4%, effective November 15.
The adjustment is expected to withdraw around $24 billion from the financial system by absorbing dollar liquidity. The move aims to slow the yuan’s appreciation after gains of more than 5% against the dollar this year, supported by strong exports, trade surpluses and corporate currency conversions.
The won’s latest advance comes after it gained around 13% against the dollar in the third quarter, its strongest quarterly rise since late 1998.
South Korea’s October exports surged 93.7% year-on-year to a record $115.28 billion, the fastest growth since January 1974, as semiconductor shipments jumped 259.4%. Inflation eased to 2.8% from 2.9%, but remained above the Bank of Korea’s 2% target.
The remaining regional calendar includes Bank Negara Malaysia’s rate decision on Thursday, where DBS expects the policy rate to remain at 2.75%, alongside October inflation readings from Taiwan, Thailand and the Philippines.

title: Trump faces midterm verdict with control of Congress at stake
full_text:
By Joseph Ax
Nov 3 (Reuters) - American voters will deliver a verdict on the first two years of President Donald Trump’s second term in Tuesday’s midterm elections, with polls and nonpartisan analysts favoring Democrats to wrest the House from Republicans while control of the Senate remains uncertain.
The battle for the Senate is unfolding across nearly 10 closely contested statewide races, most in Republican strongholds.
History is against Trump’s Republicans: the sitting president’s party has lost ground in Congress in all but two midterm elections since World War Two. Trump’s approval rating is hovering near his all-time lows, dragged down by deep voter frustration over the war with Iran and the resulting rise in fuel prices.
There is little doubt this year’s election is all about Trump, the central US political figure for most of the last decade. Trump himself has told his supporters repeatedly to "pretend I’m on the ballot," a message Democratic leaders have happily echoed.
The president has sought to energize his base with more than two dozen campaign rallies since the start of October, the vast majority in states he easily won in 2024, underscoring the extent to which Republicans are playing defense.
Led by Trump, Republicans have portrayed Democratic candidates as radical, un-American and even communist.
"The Democrat Party has nominated the most extreme and dangerous slate of candidates in American history," Trump said on Monday during a speech in Washington.
But opinion polls show voters are most concerned about affordability and disapprove of Trump’s handling of the issue, after his sweeping tariff policy and his decision to attack Iran in February increased domestic costs. Republican candidates, meanwhile, have struggled to distance themselves from a president who demands fealty and rarely acknowledges mistakes.
All 435 seats in the US House of Representatives are up for election, along with 35 of the Senate’s 100 seats, though the majority of contests are not considered competitive. Democrats must flip at least three House seats and four Senate seats to win a majority in each chamber.
A Democratic House or Senate could launch investigations into what Democrats describe as self-dealing by the Trump administration and demand concessions to approve legislation.
A Democratic Senate would also have the power to block Trump appointments, including US Supreme Court nominations if vacancies arise.
But while Democrats have put Republicans on the defensive on much of their home turf, they have little margin for error. The party must defend all of its current seats, including a tight race in Michigan, while winning at least two states that voted for Trump by a double-digit margin two years ago: Alaska, Iowa, Kansas, Nebraska, Ohio, South Carolina and Texas.
Opinion polls show Democrats either narrowly leading or within striking distance in all of those states.
MICHIGAN RACE ROILED BY CROSS-PARTY ENDORSEMENT
The Michigan Senate contest between progressive Democrat Abdul El-Sayed, 42, and Republican former US Representative Mike Rogers, 63, received a fresh jolt on Sunday, when Democrat Haley Stevens, who narrowly lost to El-Sayed in the party’s primary election, endorsed Rogers in a surprise reversal.
In addition to the implications for Senate control, the Michigan race represents a high-profile test of whether Republicans’ identity-based attacks – El-Sayed would be the nation’s first Muslim senator — prove effective in a battleground state.
A win for El-Sayed, who has criticized Israel and supports liberal policies such as universal healthcare, would also be seen as a boost for the party’s left wing ahead of the 2028 presidential election.
The Alaska Senate race has been caught up in its own turmoil, after the New York Times reported that the campaign of Democratic candidate Mary Peltola, 53, helped recruit a third candidate who shares the first and last name of her Republican opponent, Dan Sullivan, 61.
Peltola has denied involvement. Trump’s Justice Department has launched a criminal probe into the allegations and filed a lawsuit to block certification of the election results, though a judge dismissed the latter effort.
In Texas, Democratic Senate candidate James Talarico, 37, has his party once again dreaming of winning the biggest Republican state after decades of heartbreak. His scandal-plagued opponent, Republican Attorney General Ken Paxton, 63, has benefited from a nine-figure investment from the world’s richest man, Elon Musk, who has spent hundreds of millions of dollars boosting Republicans.
In Kansas, Democrat Adam Hamilton, 62, a megachurch pastor, held a narrow polling lead over Republican US Senator Roger Marshall, 66. The state voted for Trump by more than 16 percentage points in 2024 and has not elected a Democratic senator in nearly a century.
And in Maine, Republican US Senator Susan Collins, 73, is once again seeking to defy the Democratic leanings of her home state and win a sixth term. She faces Democrat Troy Jackson, 58, a former state senate president who unexpectedly became the nominee after Democratic oyster farmer Graham Platner dropped out amid accusations of misconduct, which he denied.
Other competitive Senate races are taking place in Iowa, Nebraska, Ohio and South Carolina, all Republican-held seats.
TRUMP’S JUSTICE DEPARTMENT INTERVENES
There are 47 US House races widely seen as competitive, according to a Reuters analysis of the leading election forecasters. If the other contests all proceed as predicted, Democrats would need to win only 13 of those 46 races to secure a majority.
The fight for the House has been waged largely on Republican turf, including some districts Trump carried by double digits in 2024. A Trump-backed Republican effort to redraw districts in several states to make them safer for the party appears not to have yielded the gains the White House expected.
Democrats have warned that Trump, who has long falsely claimed that US elections are rigged, may attempt to challenge Tuesday’s results if Republicans lose.
In addition to its actions in Alaska, Trump’s Justice Department also filed a lawsuit in California to block ballots it says may be invalid, a break from decades of practice meant to insulate elections from political influence. The U.S. Supreme Court on Monday rejected the administration’s request for an emergency order in the case.
Three dozen governors’ races will also take place on Tuesday, as well as thousands of state-level legislative contests and ballot measures on everything from a billionaires’ tax to abortion rights.

By Lewis Krauskopf
NEW YORK, Nov 3 (Reuters) - Investors are weighing the market implications of a possible shift in control of US Congress in Tuesday’s midterm elections, focused on whether a strong Democratic showing could pave the way for greater volatility in asset prices, particularly the AI trade which has been a main driver for markets.
The midterms come at a fragile time for markets, with a swoon in AI shares causing investor unease that could be exacerbated by the election results. Tuesday’s outcome could hold broad implications for market-sensitive areas including the AI data-center buildout, the US fiscal outlook, defense spending, and regulation in areas such as healthcare, banking and cryptocurrencies.
President Donald Trump’s Republican party has controlled both chambers of Congress during the first two years of his second term. Opinion polls show the Democrats are likely to take the House, while the Senate is too close to call.
"While probabilities increasingly favor a Blue sweep, several tightly contested Senate races leave open some possibility of Republican control of the Senate or, conversely, a greater than expected Democratic foothold in the Senate," Scott Chronert, US equity strategist at Citigroup, said in a research note. "Equity market reaction is likely positive in the former case and negative in the latter."
Strategists at UBS Global Wealth Management have assigned a 50% probability of a Democratic sweep, a 40% chance of Democrats winning the House while Republicans retain the Senate, and a 10% probability that Republicans hang onto both chambers.
"The most visible effects of a change in congressional control would likely be greater oversight of the administration and more difficult fiscal negotiations," Mark Haefele, chief investment officer at UBS Global Wealth Management, said in a note on Monday.
A Democratic-led Congress could exert greater scrutiny over AI companies, in part due to growing public opposition to data centers, a risk for a market that has been lifted by such investment spending. Many investors have said they are eager to get past the elections, which have hung over the markets for the last several weeks. Since 1970, in midterm election years, the S&P 500 index has gained in every six-month period following the election, according to Edward Jones.

Options on the S&P 500 index are priced for a move of about 0.8% in either direction on Wednesday, slightly higher than the 0.6% average implied daily move over the past month, according to ORATS data.

title: Goldman Sachs names stock winners and losers after $6.3 bln Binance heist
full_text:
Investing.com -- Goldman Sachs said the $6.3 billion hack at Binance is a net negative for the crypto stocks it covers, but that a flight to safety could help regulated firms such as Coinbase, BitGo and Robinhood.
Last week, Binance, the largest crypto exchange by trading volume, disclosed a cybersecurity incident affecting about $6.3 billion of assets, the largest crypto cyberattack to date by assets affected. Nearly $20 billion, or 14% of platform assets, has left Binance since the disclosure.
About $3 billion, mostly stablecoins, was reportedly frozen by issuers including Circle and Tether and is potentially recoverable. Withdrawals resumed Nov. 1, and Binance has committed to covering all losses.
The hack calls into question cybersecurity across the crypto ecosystem and could hurt long-term industry growth, Goldman analysts led by James Yaro said in a note. They believe that concern contributed to a 4% drop in total crypto market cap since the day before the breach.
"Overall, we view this event as a negative for our digital assets coverage, specifically in terms of lower cryptoasset balances, and potentially lower crypto trading volumes and stablecoin balances," the analysts wrote. Most affected could be BitGo, Coinbase, and Gemini, whose custody, staking, and trading businesses make up most of their revenue. Coinbase also has substantial exposure to the USDC stablecoin.
Circle, eToro, Galaxy, Robinhood, and SQN could be affected to a lesser extent, the analysts noted, because they are less directly exposed or more diversified.
Goldman also highlighted possible second-order benefits. With customer assets leaving Binance, accounts could migrate to regulated custodians and brokerages. The analysts view Coinbase, BitGo, and Robinhood as "best-positioned," citing proven cybersecurity records and substantial regulation that raises the bar for security.
Beyond individual stocks, they said the incident could slow institutional adoption of crypto, especially at heavily regulated financial institutions with limited risk tolerance. It could also raise the bar for crypto legislation, including the CLARITY Act, and increase scrutiny of cybersecurity controls for foreign exchanges seeking U.S. licenses.

title: Betting on US midterms brings rush, stress as serious money goes on the line
full_text:
By Suzanne McGee, Douglas Gillison and Chris Prentice
NEW YORK, Nov 3 (Reuters) - When polls close in the US midterm elections on Tuesday night, Noah Poser will be glued to his phone tracking dozens of large wagers he placed on prediction markets.
Poser, 28, who works in financial technology and has written about betting strategies in such markets, plans to track every change in the vote count from a friend’s watch party in New York City.
He said he has wagers with a total value in the six figures on the line, betting on a strong showing by Democrats, and entered the bets a few months ago when odds were at a much better price. If he wins, he estimates profits of as much as $30,000.
"It’s a numbers game; you have to strip your emotions out of it," said Poser, the author of a self-published book about his prediction markets strategies. Poser built a quantitative model for trading these markets based on a career in Wall Street technology systems.
He will not be alone on Tuesday evening. Across the United States, people are betting on this year’s midterm races at record levels for US election betting.
Prediction markets rose to prominence in 2024 when they bucked traditional opinion polls in signaling that Donald Trump would win the presidency. The platforms allow traders to buy and sell "yes" or "no" contracts on an array of race outcomes and variables, and there is more than $1.4 billion wagered on the midterms, according to the platforms and industry research.
SWEAT AND PANIC SELLING
Among those placing bets is Darius Gamble, 51, in Gardendale, Alabama, who said he has been betting on the platforms for two or three months but won’t wager more than $20 on anything.
"It is gambling, just disguised as predictions," said Gamble, who is a human resources business partner. "It gives you a gambling rush."
Another hopeful with money on the line is Yadin Eldar, a 22-year-old student at Florida State University.
While he anticipates large-scale Democratic victories, Eldar is opting for a contrarian strategy by placing bets on races where his analysis shows the odds of Republican candidates emerging victorious are "extremely underpriced."
"You can make a 50-55% profit on Republicans winning in Florida," he said in an interview.
Still, betting on elections is stressful, said Eldar, who may leave his own phone at home when he heads to an unrelated birthday party on Tuesday night.
"The emotional roller coaster is extremely dangerous," he said. "It never does me any good. I panic sell or panic buy."
MORE MAINSTREAM
Large-scale events are also taking advantage of the exploding interest.
A packed gathering of more than 2,000 prediction markets traders, investors and platforms in October in New York called NEXTPredict featured several sessions devoted to election contracts.
"It’s a very different vibe than we had in 2024, when prediction markets were really new and kind of upstarts," said Lucas Kohorst, co-founder of Adjacent Markets, a platform that this summer raised $2.5 million to help build out its business aggregating contracts into tradable indexes or benchmarks.
Adjacent’s Democrat Political Futures Index has climbed 2.38% in the last seven days, while its Republican counterpart has edged up 0.14%.
Late last week, Kohorst and his team decided to fly from New York to Chicago to attend an election eve watch party hosted by Kalshi, a top prediction market that joined financial market stalwarts like the Options Clearing Corporation as a silver-level sponsor of the Futures Industry Association’s annual conference.
"This time, prediction markets seem to have joined the mainstream," Kohorst said.
Kalshi did not respond to requests for comment on the event.
VEGAS
Even in Las Vegas, spiritual home to an industry that strongly opposes such platforms, prediction markets aficionados are seizing on the midterms as a way to distract gamblers from the blinking slot machines and spinning roulette wheels in the Strip’s casinos.
Peter Klamka is wagering that the elections will transform his just-launched Prediction Vegas bar into a hot new destination, as he prepares to host the Prediction Markets Conference industry gathering on Tuesday evening.
"No casinos will be showing elections," Klamka said. "From a Vegas standpoint, I’m it."
Nevada has severely restricted prediction market offerings. But Klamka says many of his out-of-state clientele make their trades before arriving.
That’s why Ish Milly, the organizer of the Vegas prediction markets conference, sees the election party as only one small part of the story.
"Ultimately, we’re more interested in the long-term development and credibility of the industry than the outcome of any single election," he said.

title: Goldman lifts natural gas price forecasts on supply, weather uncertainty
full_text:
Investing.com -- Goldman Sachs raised its European natural gas price forecasts, flagging a still highly uncertain outlook for Middle East liquefied natural gas (LNG) supply and winter weather, and said risks to its 2027 projections remain skewed to the upside.
The bank lifted its first-quarter 2027 TTF forecast to €74 per megawatt-hour from €44, and its 2027 average to €51 from €32.
The increase reflects a subjective 45% probability of a low-supply winter for Middle East LNG, worth €26 in the first quarter, plus a small cold-weather risk component worth €4, analyst Samantha Dart said.
The forecasts remain below forwards, at €92 for the first quarter and €69 for summer 2027. Goldman said the first-quarter forward implies a 47% market-perceived probability of a very tight scenario.
TTF prices fell sharply Monday from Friday’s €104 close as headlines pointed to a possible diplomatic attempt, partially reversing earlier concerns about military escalation after the U.S. midterms, while short-range weather models turned more neutral.
"The range of outcomes for TTF this winter remains exceptionally wide," Dart said.
In Goldman’s base case, Persian Gulf LNG exports climb gradually to an operating maximum of 83% of normal by February. Qatar damaged 17% of its export capacity earlier this year and has guided to a multi-year repair.
Exports averaged 33% of pre-war levels in October, 13 percentage points above Goldman’s base case, though recent days have seen lower flows through Hormuz.
If exports stay at 25% to 30% of normal through March and the winter in northwest Europe is one standard deviation colder than average, Goldman estimates first-quarter TTF would approach €150.
A warmer winter and improved supply would drop it to €45, which would essentially halt European competition for LNG with the rest of the world, Dart noted.
Demand destruction could help Europe preserve gas storage, she said, but at a cost. Goldman estimates 2027 TTF would need to average €70 if Gulf exports stay restricted through the winter, and €104 if they stay below 35% of normal through 2027.
Dart said some of the upside risk is priced in, but that the recent drop in Hormuz LNG flows still favors hedging a tight winter through first-quarter 2027 TTF call spreads.
Longer term, the analyst said LNG balances look "increasingly soft" given recent additional export capacity decisions.

title: New cyberattack on supermarket fridges sweeps across Europe
full_text:
By Marie Mannes, Helen Reid and Louise Rasmussen
STOCKHOLM/BRUSSELS/LONDON, Nov 2 (Reuters) - A hacking attack on European supermarkets spread across the continent on Monday, hitting fridges and freezers from Sweden to Belgium and forcing stores to throw away food in an incident that echoed a similar attack in France last month.
The attack, which raised temperatures in refrigerator and freezer units at dozens of stores, hit supermarket groups Ahold Delhaize and Colruyt in Belgium and Luxembourg, as well as Swedish grocers ICA and Coop. Furniture-to-meatballs retailer IKEA also saw at least one store affected.
"Everything is destroyed," Engla Ingwall, sales manager at an ICA franchise store in Stockholm, told Reuters during a visit to the store on Monday, adding the attack occurred at 2 a.m. (0100 GMT) but was only noticed hours later.
"There has been a cyberattack and all our freezers reached 50 degrees (Celsius)."
A spokesperson for privately held ICA said the company was aware that a "limited number of stores were affected by an incident overnight, which impacted their refrigeration and freezer systems".
The latest incidents follow an attack in France last month when police said hackers seized control of cooling units at hundreds of supermarkets, causing fires and food losses. Ahold also reported a cybersecurity incident to police last month.
While no one has claimed responsibility for either attack, the incidents have heightened concerns among European authorities about hybrid threats to infrastructure amid growing security tensions since Russia’s 2022 invasion of Ukraine.
Moscow has repeatedly denied involvement in sabotage or hybrid warfare operations. Reuters could not establish who was behind Monday’s attacks or whether they were linked to the incidents in France.
"It is not known who is behind this attack, and it may never be determined," said Katrien Eggers, spokesperson for Belgium’s Centre for Cybersecurity, adding she was concerned about the growing number of incidents, in part due to AI.
"All IT systems are potentially vulnerable, and AI can now be used to successfully exploit these weaknesses — especially by sophisticated actors," she said.
’RETAIL IS AN EASY TARGET’
From refrigerators and heating systems to security cameras and alarms, an expanding range of devices once largely mechanical can now be monitored and controlled remotely, creating new opportunities for cybercriminals.
At least some of the refrigerator units affected on Monday used temperature control technology from Danish firm Danfoss that was also targeted in the French attack. The firm said it had been working with customers to implement fixes.
The European Commission said the latest incidents highlighted how digital threats are becoming increasingly disruptive.
"They are a deliberate attempt to disrupt our food supply chain and undermine consumers’ confidence in it – a warning that we must take seriously," said EU commissioner for agriculture Christophe Hansen. "The repeated occurrence of these cyberattacks is deeply concerning."
A spokesperson for Colruyt Group, which operates Spar stores in Belgium under a franchise system, said five shops had their fridge systems attacked.
In Ireland, wholesaler Musgrave said the incident affected systems in 13 of its SuperValu stores, forcing it to remove some chilled and frozen products from sale.
"Our monitoring systems alerted us to the issue and we took immediate action," it said in a statement. "Our investigation is ongoing."
Tom Hegel, a researcher at cybersecurity firm SentinelOne, said such attacks were typically linked to extortion, political motives or nation-state operations, with the absence of financial demands in recent cases pointing instead to sabotage.
"Retail is an easy target because retail chains run enormous estates of refrigeration controllers, building management systems, door access panels and point-of-sale gear," he said, adding it was hard to trace hackers targeting such systems.
"An attacker who logs into an exposed control panel leaves almost nothing behind ... A teenager and an intelligence service would look much the same from the defender’s side."
’IT’S VERY SCARY’
Carrefour, which was badly hit in last month’s French attack, said 15 of its 700 stores in Belgium were affected. IKEA said one store in Belgium had been impacted and that it could not rule out disruptions at other locations.
Privately held Swedish grocery chain Coop said that 7 of its 800 stores were affected by a cyber incident involving unauthorised tampering with its refrigeration systems. It said Danfoss was among its suppliers.
Luc De Laet, founder and owner of Belgian butchery chain De Laet & Van Haver, said he was woken at 3:30 a.m. by an employee telling him there was a problem. He rushed to his store south of Antwerp and found the fridges turned up as high as 18 C.
He estimated the incident ruined about €15,000 ($16,800) worth of meat.
"It’s very scary. They are hacking the system that is doing the registration of the temperature, and they can program it at a distance," he told Reuters, adding that it was infuriating to throw away so much food.
De Laet said he believed the hackers were trying to destabilise European economies. He had contacted police but did not know whether an investigation had been launched.
"I only have two words for them: wake up, please, because there’s something going on," he said.

Opinion polls and nonpartisan analysts favor Democrats to wrest the House of Representatives from Republicans, while Senate control remains uncertain.
Brent futures fell $1.63, or 2%, to $103.14 a barrel at 10:44 a.m. ET (1544 GMT), while US West Texas Intermediate crude fell 67 cents, or 1%, to $95.79.
Brent was on track for its lowest close since October 7 and WTI was headed for its lowest close since October 14.
Iran and the United States are still far from a deal to end their war, a senior Iranian official told Reuters, while mediator Qatar stepped up efforts to bridge differences and avert a renewed escalation after the US midterm elections.
Qatar’s Foreign Ministry spokesperson said the US and Iran remain committed to mediation efforts and are reviewing proposals aimed at bridging their differences.
"Despite these positive signals, it’s probably too early to think escalation risks have passed," ING said in a note. "What is clear, though, is that strong signals of progress in peace talks would mean more downside for prices."
Overnight, the US carried out strikes on Iran’s Qeshm Island, with a US official saying the strikes targeted surface-to-air missiles used against US assets. Another official said the strikes appeared limited and did not signal a return to major combat operations.
Separately, Trump said he made a deal with Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu that Washington would stop $4 billion in funding to Israel after the end of this year.
Saudi state oil company Aramco is working to expand a crude pipeline that circumvents the Strait of Hormuz, CEO Amin Nasser said.
The effective blockade of the chokepoint that links the Gulf to world markets, previously a conduit for 20% of global oil supplies, has redrawn energy flows and infrastructure investment priorities among the region’s oil producers.
RUSSIA AND UKRAINE
Russia will hold three-way peace talks with Ukraine and the United States in Abu Dhabi from November 10 to 11, the Kremlin confirmed.
Russia was the world’s third-biggest crude oil producer behind the US and Saudi Arabia in 2025, US energy data showed. Sanctions designed to keep Russian energy out of global markets after Moscow’s invasion of Ukraine have helped support oil prices.
Any deal to end Russia’s invasion of Ukraine, which Moscow launched in 2022, could allow Russia to export more.
Ahead of the upcoming talks, however, Russia bombarded Ukraine’s energy infrastructure, knocking out power to swathes of the country with dozens of missiles and hundreds of drones.
Ukraine set fire to a major oil refinery in the Russian city of Yaroslavl in an overnight drone attack, the regional governor said.
Recent attacks on cargo ships near NATO members Romania and Bulgaria show how the escalating maritime war between Russia and Ukraine is expanding into a major challenge for NATO in the Black Sea.
US OIL STOCKPILES
The oil market is awaiting weekly storage reports from the American Petroleum Institute trade group on Tuesday and the US Energy Information Administration on Wednesday.
Analysts estimate energy firms added 2 million barrels of crude to US storage during the week ended October 30.

title: Exclusive-US billionaire leads swap plan to buy Lukoil’s overseas assets, sources say
full_text:
By Anna Hirtenstein, Timour Azhari and Jarrett Renshaw
LONDON, Nov 3 (Reuters) - A consortium led by US billionaire Todd Boehly is preparing a securities swap to acquire sanctioned Russian oil major Lukoil’s international assets and a deal is expected within weeks, four people close to the sales process said.
A bank acting on behalf of the consortium has purchased billions of dollars of frozen Lukoil securities from Western investment funds to exchange for the company’s foreign assets, three of the people said.
The people declined to be identified because they are not authorised to discuss the matter publicly.
If completed, the transaction would conclude a sale process that has dragged on for more than a year and initially valued the portfolio involved at $22 billion. Lukoil’s foreign assets include oilfields, refineries and petrol stations in Europe, the Middle East and Africa.
The value of the portfolio has deteriorated as some assets have stopped operating, two people said.
A deal would also test whether Western sanctions can compel a major Russian company to divest international assets while keeping strategic oil operations and limiting financial gains to Moscow.
The consortium includes Boehly, a Miami-based businessman who owns stakes in Los Angeles sports teams the Dodgers and the Lakers, and Emirati investors International Holding Company (IHC) and Al Hail Holding. The Syrian-Qatari Al-Khayat brothers and the US International Development Finance Corp (DFC) are also backing the bid.
Representatives of Boehly did not respond to multiple requests for comment. An IHC spokesperson said they do not comment on potential investment activities. Al Hail, the Al-Khayats and the US DFC did not respond to requests for comment.
Lukoil did not immediately respond to a request for comment.
The plan is for a cashless deal in which frozen Lukoil securities held by Western investors, including Capital Group, would be exchanged for Lukoil’s international assets, the people said.
Capital Group declined to comment.
INITIAL OFFER REJECTED
The sale process started following US sanctions on Lukoil in October 2025. Reuters reported in February that the US slowed the sale partly to pressure Russia in negotiations to end its war in Ukraine.
Last December, the US Treasury rejected an offer from a group that included US bank Xtellus Partners saying that Lukoil should not receive a windfall from the sale in shares or cash.
The Boehly-led consortium was able to move forward by promising to put the shares in an escrow account, rather than transferring them straight to Lukoil, two people said. The US Treasury did not respond to requests for comment.
More than a dozen companies bid for Lukoil’s assets, including oil majors Exxon Mobil and Chevron, US private equity group Carlyle, and the former owner of Pornhub Bernd Bergmair, Reuters reported in November last year. Carlyle dropped out of the race last month, leaving the Boehly consortium in the lead.
LUKOIL SECURITIES BOUGHT FROM US, UK FUNDS
The bank acting on behalf of the consortium bought Lukoil securities from around 10 US and British investment funds as well as US depositary banks which held them on behalf of retail investors, two of the people said.
The shares were priced at 30 cents on the dollar, the other two people said, a substantial discount that reflected their sanctioned status.
Western investment funds were large holders of Lukoil stock before Russia’s 2022 invasion of Ukraine. The shares were subsequently removed from major emerging market indices and have since been frozen and written down by Western funds.

title: European supermarkets rush to patch vulnerabilities after region-wide fridge hack
full_text:
By Louise Rasmussen, Helen Reid and Marcus Mathiesen
COPENHAGEN/LONDON, Nov 3 (Reuters) - European supermarkets targeted in a second wave of cyberattacks that cranked up fridge and freezer temperatures were rushing on Tuesday to upgrade their systems and protect themselves against further hacking attempts.
Stores in eight European countries were forced to throw away vast quantities of food after hackers tampered on Monday with their fridges, in an attack identical to one that swept dozens of supermarkets in France three weeks ago.
In Sweden, supermarket chain Coop said it was switching systems to 5G networks and modern modems, instead of 4G connections - a process that had already started since the French incident.
The seven stores hit by the attack are back up and running but their refrigeration systems have been disconnected from the internet, a spokesperson said.
"We are looking quite thoroughly and deeply into the status of the entire network of stores to see if we risk any vulnerability anywhere in the entire network," the spokesperson added.
Software provider Danfoss, whose systems were again among those targeted, said it has been in close contact with customers over the past three weeks to help them manage the situation, and recommended that systems should not be directly accessible via the internet.
“Retailers need to act now. They should identify whether their refrigerator controllers are vulnerable, check if they are connected to the internet, ensure they’ve got the latest security updates and are supported by the manufacturer. And if they don’t even know, then remove them from the public internet immediately,” said Frank Groenewegen, cybersecurity expert at Deloitte in The Hague.
“With disconnecting, you haven’t fixed the root cause but you’ve at least isolated those systems so that an attacker is not able to do this anymore.”
’HEIGHTENED ALERT’
Many European supermarkets are run by independent business owners in a cooperative structure, meaning systems are not the same across stores.
Swedish grocer ICA said all 23 stores hit in Monday’s cyberattack had equipment connected outside the chain’s centrally managed store network.
ICA store owner Christian Olofsson said he felt even more frustrated about the cyberattack given he was in the process of changing the security systems at his stores in Tomelilla and Sjobo in Sweden when they were hacked.
A Swedish police spokesperson said around 10 police reports had been filed since Monday and they expected more.
German supermarket operator Edeka, which had fridges hacked at a store in Reisbach, Germany, told Reuters there are no standardised refrigeration systems across its network of stores run by independent retailers.
Even integrated supermarket groups were not immune: Carrefour, which had 80 franchised stores in France hacked three weeks ago, suffered the same cyberattack again at 15 stores in Belgium on Monday.
EU cybersecurity agency ENISA said the large-scale nature of the cyberattacks targeting retail across several member states "underscores the importance of European cooperation, rapid information-sharing and coordinated responses to cyber incidents".
In Britain, hackers tried to target small meat-processing firms but the impact was minimal, said Richard Horne, chief executive of the National Cyber Security Centre (NCSC).
The NCSC is working with organisations to spot vulnerabilities and close them before somebody exploits them, Horne said. "We’re obviously on heightened alert."
The attack on supermarket fridges is just an early sign of what are likely to be increasingly frequent disruptions as old technology fails to keep pace with hackers, Horne said.

title: AI spending boom could exceed $10 trillion, raising fears of financial fallout
full_text:
Investing.com --The scale of the artificial intelligence investment boom is becoming a source of concern, with spending on infrastructure potentially exceeding $10 trillion if companies follow through on their current plans.
Bill Dudley, former president of the Federal Reserve Bank of New York, warned in a Bloomberg Opinion article that the race to build AI capacity risks creating an industry with far more infrastructure than it can ultimately support.
At least seven or eight companies are pursuing ambitions to become major AI hyperscalers, but Dudley believes only two or three may emerge as dominant players. The economics of cloud computing, where scale and network effects favor a handful of large providers, could play out similarly in AI.
That raises questions about whether the industry can generate enough revenue to justify the enormous capital commitments. Given the rapid depreciation of data centers and computing equipment, Dudley estimates that AI infrastructure could require more than $3 trillion in annual revenue to deliver an adequate return on investment.
The potential fallout goes beyond technology stocks. A reversal in spending could hit equity markets hard, while also exposing lenders and investors that have financed the infrastructure buildout.
Dudley does not see a repeat of the 2008 financial crisis as the most likely outcome. Unlike the mortgage market ahead of the global financial crisis, risks surrounding AI investment are already widely discussed. Financing also tends to be longer-term, making a sudden wave of forced asset sales less likely.
Still, there are reasons for caution. Much of the funding comes from private credit and leasing arrangements, making it difficult to establish exactly who is exposed and under what conditions. Some obligations also remain off balance sheet until data center projects are completed.
Nvidia’s guarantees of future chip values present another potential vulnerability. If those guarantees are triggered as chip prices fall, the company could face additional financial pressure precisely when its margins are already coming under strain.
Dudley is calling for regulators to improve disclosure of financing arrangements and contingent liabilities, arguing that investors need a clearer picture of the risks building beneath the AI spending boom.
The investment cycle may not end in another financial crisis, but the amount of capital involved makes the consequences of a sharp correction difficult to dismiss.

title: Trump’s DOJ sends election monitors overwhelmingly to Democratic areas
full_text:
By Dan Rosenzweig-Ziff and Doina Chiacu
WASHINGTON, Nov 3 (Reuters) - The US Justice Department deployed officials on Tuesday across the country to monitor midterm voting in predominately Democratic jurisdictions while widening a criminal probe into an Alaska campaign for a US Senate seat.
The department announced it was sending 1,000 election monitors and observers to jurisdictions in all 50 states. Democrat Kamala Harris defeated President Donald Trump in about two-thirds of those jurisdictions in the 2024 presidential election, a Reuters analysis found.
Black and Latino voters make up a majority in many of the juridictions, which are concentrated in states that could determine control of the US Senate.
The Trump administration has taken an aggressive approach to election oversight, pressing states for voter-registration data and arguing that stricter measures are needed to ensure public confidence in the vote.
That has included asking the Supreme Court to temporarily block California from counting mail-in ballots from more than 20,000 voters, who federal officials allege are likely noncitizens. The Supreme Court rejected that appeal Monday night. Critics have called those actions and the monitoring program potential voter intimidation.
In Alaska, the Senate race was thrown into turmoil after the New York Times reported last week that the campaign of Democratic candidate Mary Peltola helped recruit a third candidate who shares the first and last name of her Republican opponent, Dan Sullivan. Peltola has denied involvement.
The Justice Department has launched a criminal probe into the allegations, an investigation it is widening.
The department is sending letters to more than 20 people notifying them that they are subjects of the criminal probe, according to a person familiar with the investigation who spoke on the condition of anonymity to talk about it.
One of the recipients is voting rights lawyer Marc Elias, whose law firm frequently represents Democrats in court, the person said.
“No one should be surprised that President Trump’s Department of Justice is targeting me and my law firm on Election Day," Elias said in a statement. "This administration has repeatedly weaponized the DOJ against the President’s political enemies despite zero evidence of wrongdoing, and we are the latest targets."
’LARGEST MONITORING EFFORT IN DOJ HISTORY’
The Justice Department has long sent monitors to states to observe elections, and senior officials have said they were dispatching observers to ensure compliance with federal law in areas where voters have historically had access issues and could face intimidation efforts in competitive races.
“I am very proud we are deploying the largest monitoring effort in DOJ history, and pursuing transparency for elections in an assertive and nondiscriminatory manner,” said Assistant Attorney General Harmeet K. Dhillon in a statement.
The expanded federal monitoring program led several states to issue new guidelines to local election officials and poll workers about the limited authority DOJ observers will have on Election Day.
Some jurisdictions, including Hennepin County, Minnesota, which includes Minneapolis, have denied Justice Department requests for access to polling places. DOJ staff cannot conduct investigations on the spot or otherwise stop anyone from voting.

title: Apple’s ’unprecedented’ memory warning adds fuel to wobbly Micron, SK hynix trade
full_text:
Investing.com -- Apple (NASDAQ:AAPL) may have delivered one of the clearest warnings yet that the global memory squeeze has further to run, giving investors another reason to watch Micron (NASDAQ:MU), SK hynix (NASDAQ:SKHY) and Samsung Electronics Co Ltd (KS:005930).
On its earnings call Monday, Apple CEO John Ternus described memory pricing as “unprecedented” and said the prices the company pays will keep climbing beyond the December quarter. As one of the world’s biggest buyers of memory for iPhones, Macs and iPads, Apple offers a window into pricing pressure well beyond AI data centers.
The impact is already showing up in Apple’s margins. The company forecast December quarter gross margin of 45% to 46%, down from 47.9% in September. Chief Financial Officer Kevan Parekh said most of the decline would be driven by higher memory costs. Excluding tariff effects, memory accounted for the entire one percentage point sequential margin decline from June to September.
Management does not see relief around the corner. Ternus said Apple paid more for memory in September than in June and expects costs to rise further in the December quarter. Looking beyond that period, memory purchase prices are expected to keep increasing. Apple has raised prices on Macs, iPads and iPhones to help offset the pressure. Carry-in inventory and lower costs for some non-memory components are providing relief, but the benefit from older inventory is expected to fade.
The pressure is not just about cost. Apple said Mac and iPad supply will remain constrained in the December quarter, primarily because of memory, as demand has exceeded expectations. The company’s manufacturing purchase obligations increased by $33 billion between June and September as it works to improve supply. Those commitments cover broader manufacturing needs, not memory alone, but underscore the effort to secure components.
For memory makers, Apple’s comments confirm suppliers’ pricing power. AI infrastructure spending has encouraged chipmakers to prioritize high-bandwidth memory and server products, tightening supplies of conventional DRAM used in phones and computers. TrendForce expects conventional DRAM contract prices to rise 10% to 15% in the fourth quarter, while NAND flash prices are forecast to climb 15% to 20%.
Yet the memory trade has become more complicated. Despite the strong supply-demand backdrop, Micron, SK hynix, Samsung and other memory-related stocks have pulled sharply back from recent highs as investors worry China could eventually add enough capacity to disrupt the market. China’s largest DRAM maker, ChangXin Memory Technologies, or CXMT, is expanding conventional memory production and moving into advanced AI memory, raising concerns that new Chinese supply could weaken pricing power.
Those fears have helped drive a sharp sector selloff. Micron fell sharply in late October as investors reacted to renewed concerns about CXMT, while SK hynix and Samsung were among the hardest-hit stocks during an earlier October chip rout. The concern is not that Chinese suppliers are already matching industry leaders, but that they could become a more meaningful competitor over time.
The near-term gap remains substantial. Reuters reported last week that CXMT plans to begin limited production of HBM3E, an advanced memory chip used with AI processors, despite yields of only 20% to 30%, compared with about 70% at SK hynix. Testing also suggested CXMT’s product remains closer to an earlier generation of HBM. China therefore represents a longer-term risk, not an immediate replacement for established suppliers.
For now, Apple has added a powerful new data point to the bullish memory thesis: AI demand is not only driving shortages of specialized chips in data centers. It is also making memory inside everyday consumer devices more expensive and harder to secure. The question for investors is how long that imbalance can last before new supply, particularly from China, changes the equation.

title: CFTC approves trading of single-stock perpetual futures under joint SEC oversight
full_text:
Investing.com -- The Commodity Futures Trading Commission has authorized the launch of perpetual futures tied to single stocks, opening domestic markets to an around-the-clock, leveraged trading instrument previously confined largely to offshore crypto platforms. Approved as security futures products under the Commodity Futures Modernization Act, the contracts will be traded on designated contract markets dually registered with the Securities and Exchange Commission, subjecting them to joint oversight from both regulatory agencies.
The landmark clearance represents the latest phase of a coordinated campaign by regulators to onshore popular non-expiring derivatives, following the agency’s green light for bitcoin perpetual contracts earlier this year. CFTC Chairman Michael Selig emphasized that the move brings widely sought price-discovery and risk-management tools onto domestic venues, ending years of interagency jurisdictional gridlock that left such instruments stranded in regulatory limbo.
The contracts differ fundamentally from conventional equity derivatives by eliminating fixed expiration dates and enabling continuous trading outside traditional exchange hours. While international volume has demonstrated massive demand for continuous leveraged exposure, critics contend that the products introduce severe systemic and consumer risks to less sophisticated retail participants.
The regulatory breakthrough arrives against a backdrop of mounting bipartisan pushback on Capitol Hill over potential investor vulnerabilities and jurisdictional oversight. Republican Senator Katie Britt previously urged regulators to guarantee robust investor safeguards, while a coalition of six Democratic senators recently pressed the SEC to maintain exclusive control over equity derivatives and clarify its market surveillance mechanisms.
Pushback escalated swiftly following Tuesday’s announcement, with Senate Banking Committee ranking member Elizabeth Warren sharply rebuking the agency’s authorization in a statement, saying, "This kind of risky financial product is ripe for insider trading, puts American investors at risk, and could inject serious volatility into our markets." The joint regulatory framework is poised to face intensified congressional scrutiny in the coming year, particularly if Democrats reclaim control of the House or Senate.

The latest deliberations come as CVS faces pressure across both its insurance and pharmacy-benefit operations.
Pharmacy benefit managers are facing growing political and regulatory scrutiny on concerns that healthcare consolidation has given these companies, which act as middlemen in the drug supply chain, too much influence over prescription drug prices.
At the same time, health insurers have struggled with rising medical costs over the past three years as consumers increased their use of healthcare services, prompting companies to raise prices, cut benefits and exit less profitable plans.
CVS executive Prem Shah said in August that Caremark expects to lose clients in 2027 after taking a more cautious approach to signing contracts.
CVS Health has greater exposure to vertical integration than its peers because it owns both Caremark, one of the country’s largest pharmacy benefit managers, and a major retail pharmacy chain, Julie Utterback, an analyst at Morningstar, said.
Separating the businesses could, however, come at a cost.
"A potential spinoff faces some financial consequences, like the potential for lost synergies and new corporate standup costs," Utterback said.
Shares of CVS have rebounded under Joyner, who took over in October 2024, helping lift the company’s market value to about $117 billion.

title: 3M commits $7.35 bln over 9 years to settle PFAS foam injury claims
full_text:
Investing.com-- 3M said on Tuesday it has agreed to settle the bulk of personal injury claims in the sprawling U.S. litigation over PFAS “forever chemicals” in firefighting foam, committing $7.35 billion over nine years.
The payments have a present value of $5.8 billion, which 3M will book as a pre-tax charge in the fourth quarter. The company said the charge is a special item and leaves its 2026 guidance unchanged.
The deal covers about 99% of current claims, involving 115,000-120,000 eligible plaintiffs inside and outside the federal multidistrict litigation in South Carolina, 3M said.

title: CVS Health to split into two publicly traded companies by 2028, FT reports
full_text:
Investing.com-- CVS Health Corp (NYSE:CVS) is planning to split its retail pharmacy business from its insurance operations, potentially unwinding one of the U.S. healthcare industry's largest vertical integration deals, the Financial Times reported on Tuesday, citing people familiar with the matter.
Under plans being discussed, CVS would spin off its roughly 9,000 drugstores into a separate publicly traded company, while insurer Aetna and pharmacy-benefit manager Caremark would remain together, the report said.
The retail pharmacy division is projected to generate about a third of CVS's $417 billion in revenue this year, the FT reported.
The proposed restructuring would reverse CVS's $78 billion acquisition of Aetna in 2018, amid mounting political pressure to separate pharmacy-benefit managers from pharmacies and insurers.
The company could announce the move alongside its third-quarter results, although the structure and timeline remain subject to change, the report said.
